newsitem.title: USA: No change in policy seen with Fed seekers-Broaddus.
newsitem.headline: No change in policy seen with Fed seekers-Broaddus.

text.p: The expected nomination of two new members to the Federal Reserve Board is not expected to change the course of central bank monetary policy, said the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Alfred Broaddus.

"I don't expect any major change in policy," Broaddus said about the likely nomination of Edward Gramlich, an economist at the University of Michigan, and Roger Ferguson, a partner with consulting firm McKinsey & Co Inc, for the two vacant spots at the Fed Board.

Ferguson and Gramlich are currently undergoing background checks. No problems have cropped up so far and given that none emerges, President Bill Clinton may choose to make a formal nomination of the two candidates, U.S. officials said.
The two economists would then have to be confirmed by the U.S. Senate, which must approve the White House appointments for the Federal Reserve Board.
The president of the Richmond Fed also said consumer spending in the U.S. is firm.
"Consumer spending is specially strong, much stronger than anticipated," Broaddus told an audience of financial executives here.
Broaddus also said the state of the U.S. economy is strong, adding that there was no reason why the current economic expansion could not last longer.

"The current condition of the economy is pretty good, in many ways it's about as good as it gets," Broaddus said, adding that "There is no reason why this expansion can't continue through 1997 and beyond."
Citing a consensus of forecasters, the Richmond Fed chief said the economy is likely to grow at a somewhat slower pace in 1997 compared to 1996.
"Real (Gross Domestic Product) GDP growth could diminish from a little over 3.0 percent annual rate in 1996 to 2.5 percent in 1997," Broaddus said.
Broaddus also reiterated that the U.S. unemployment rate may slide to 5.0 percent by year end.
The latest government figures show the U.S. unemployment rate was at 5.2 percent in March.
Broaddus also said firm job growth in the U.S. combined with a wealth effect from investments in the stock market was bolstering the nation's consumer spending.
